conclusion.justification: The report notes that while older, lower-quality trials suggested a benefit, the highest-quality recent evidence (including an updated 2020 Cochrane review and large RCTs) leans toward 'little or no effect' and shows no clear benefit for shortening diarrhea duration.
conclusion.label: leans_reject

report:
**Conclusion: The most reliable evidence does not support a "no" answer as clear-cut—it's mixed, and the highest-quality, most recent evidence leans toward "little or no effect."**

Older meta-analyses (e.g., Cochrane's 2010 review) reported that probiotics shortened diarrhea duration by roughly 24-25 hours (https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD003048.pub3/abstract), and this finding has been widely cited since, including in synthesis by TheNNT (https://thennt.com/nnt/probiotics-for-acute-infectious-diarrhea/). However, that evidence base was dominated by smaller, often lower-quality trials.

Critically, the updated 2020 Cochrane review found that probiotics "may not affect how long acute diarrhoea lasts," concluding uncertainty about any meaningful benefit on recovery time (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD003048_do-probiotics-help-treat-acute-infectious-diarrhoea; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33295643/). This revision reflects inclusion of larger, more rigorous trials that diluted the earlier positive signal.

This shift is reinforced by two large, well-designed multicenter RCTs in children with acute gastroenteritis presenting to emergency departments: the NEJM 2018 trial found a combination Lactobacillus probiotic did not reduce the severity or duration of illness (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1802597), and the PECARN trial of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG similarly found no improvement in outcomes (https://pecarn.org/pecarn_news/probiotics-do-not-improve-the-outcomes-in-pediatric-acute-gastroenteritis/).

**Bottom line:** While earlier, smaller studies suggested probiotics could shorten diarrhea duration by about a day, the largest and most rigorous recent trials and the updated Cochrane review show no clear benefit. The "no" answer is well-supported by current high-quality evidence, though the field's overall picture has evolved from cautious optimism to skepticism.
